title: Orcas Turn Sunfish Into Piñatas, Scientists Discover
summary:
Orcas are known for brutal hunting tactics — slapping stingrays, punting seals into the air, and otherwise playing with their food. Now scientists have documented something even stranger: orcas smashing sunfish like piñatas.

In 2024 and 2025, researchers watched this behavior in the Gulf of California. In both cases, one adult orca held a dead sharp-tail sunfish steady. A second orca then slammed into it with enough force to smash the fish to smithereens. The findings appeared July 23 in Frontiers in Ethology.

"I was absolutely gobsmacked," said Marianne Nyegaard, a marine biologist at Auckland Museum in New Zealand who wasn't involved in the study. "I thought it was the coolest thing I had ever seen." She had seen a few social media videos of orcas battering sunfish, but the new paper does a deep dive into the behavior.

Nyegaard isn't surprised that orcas found a creative way to handle sharp-tail sunfish. Those massive fish can reach a few meters — about 10 feet — long. "Orcas will do all sorts of things," she said. "They are so clever at figuring out how to hunt and deal with a ton of different prey types."

Hunting is often a team sport for orcas. They band together to ambush blue whales and whale sharks, and they team up to make waves that knock penguins off ice.

Why pulverize a sunfish? Francesca Pancaldi, a marine biologist at Mexico's National Polytechnic Institute, says orcas most likely smash them into small pieces to help feed their young. After one of the explosions described in the paper, a young orca fed on the small bits.

But feeding may not be the only reason. "Killer whales are highly social animals," Pancaldi said. A single activity can provide nutrition, help orcas bond, and offer a way for young orcas to learn how to hunt.
why_it_matters: The story shows that animal intelligence is not only about tool use: what can look like violence or play may actually be learned, shared culture passed from adult orcas to calves, which raises hard questions about how humans manage — and how much we still don't understand — in the ocean.

background_read: Orcas, also called killer whales, are the largest members of the dolphin family and live in every ocean from the tropics to the poles. Ethology — the scientific study of animal behaviour — is the field behind this paper, which appeared in the peer-reviewed journal Frontiers in Ethology.

The Gulf of California, also known as the Sea of Cortez, is the narrow sea between Mexico's Baja California peninsula and the mainland. It is one of the most biologically rich seas on Earth and a well-known home for whales, dolphins and other marine mammals.
Marianne Nyegaard works at Auckland Museum (a natural-history museum in New Zealand) and has studied sunfish for years, which is why her reaction carries weight.

Orcas live in separate populations called ecotypes that specialise in different prey — some eat fish, others hunt seals or whales — and their hunting techniques are passed from mother to calf, something scientists describe as animal culture.

Sunfish are the heaviest bony fish in the ocean, and in recent years a population of orcas off Spain and Portugal has been ramming and even sinking small boats, behaviour researchers connect to play or social learning rather than hunger.

perspectives.perspective: Positive — the researchers and marine scientists
perspectives.description: This is the first detailed scientific description of the behaviour, turning scattered social-media clips into real data. It highlights how flexible orcas are, and the vivid image of a sunfish 'piñata' draws public attention to a species few people think about.

perspectives.perspective: Critical — cautious scientists and welfare-minded observers
perspectives.description: Only two incidents were observed, which is a thin basis for conclusions about the behaviour's purpose; calling it 'bonding' or 'teaching' risks reading human motives into animals. Others question whether boats and observers change what orcas do, and note that a smashed sunfish is a dead fish either way.

Orcas are cultural animals: different populations have different diets and inherited hunting techniques. Smashing a slow, large, energy-rich sunfish into bite-sized pieces may simply be an efficient way to turn an awkward meal into food a calf can eat.

Long-term monitoring, drones and reports from whale-watching boats could show whether this trick spreads to other orcas — the test of whether it is culture. If ocean conditions push sunfish and orcas into closer contact, such encounters could become more common.
